title: Eight Thousand Handshakes
subtitle: New Year's Day at the White House
intro: For most of the nineteenth century and a good stretch of the twentieth, the White House opened its doors on New Year's Day and anybody willing to stand in the queue could shake the president's hand. On 1 January 1907 an awful lot of people did. Ten questions on the most exhausting tradition in American public life.
heroAlt: Members of the public filing in to the White House for the New Year's reception
heroCredit: General public being admitted to the White House for the New Year's reception. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What happened at the White House every New Year's Day in Roosevelt's time?
options: A military review and parade on the South Lawn
A public reception open to all comers
Nothing — the house was shut to visitors all day
A private dinner for the cabinet, and no public admitted
questions.explanation: The doors opened and the public came in — no ticket, no invitation, nothing required but the willingness to stand in the queue and shake the president's hand at the end of it. Officials and diplomats went first by protocol, but behind them stretched a line of ordinary citizens down the avenue, and every one of them got a handshake. It is hard now to picture a head of state standing for hours in a room letting several thousand strangers take hold of his hand.
questions.imageAlt: Crowd waiting in line outside the White House for the New Year's reception
questions.credit: Crowd waiting in line outside of the White House for the New Year's reception. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: On 1 January 1907, roughly how many hands did Roosevelt shake?
options: None — he cancelled that year
About five hundred
More than eight thousand
About eighty thousand
questions.explanation: More than eight thousand, in a single day. The exact figure has never been settled: the New York Sun said ten thousand, the Evening Star said 5,063, the Washington Herald counted 8,513, the New York Tribune 8,500 and the Guinness book later settled on 8,150. Everyone who was actually there agreed it was somewhere north of eight thousand.
questions.imageAlt: The public being admitted to the White House on New Year's Day
questions.credit: General public being admitted to the White House for the New Year's reception. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What did that day earn him?
options: A formal complaint from the diplomatic corps
A rebuke from his doctor
A bandaged right arm for a fortnight
A world record for handshakes by a head of state
questions.explanation: The record for most handshakes by a head of state, and it stood for the better part of a century. His biographer's verdict on the day is worth keeping: never again would Roosevelt, or any other president, enjoy quite that much homage.
questions.credit: The White House, Washington, D.C., 1905. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Who came through the receiving line first?
options: Foreign ambassadors
White House staff
Newspaper correspondents
Members of the public
questions.explanation: Strict protocol: foreign ambassadors, then the justices of the Supreme Court, then senators, representatives, and army and navy officers — and only then the several thousand ordinary citizens who made up the bulk of the day. Edith stood beside him for all of it in white corded silk.
questions.imageAlt: Admiral Dewey and naval officers in line for the 1902 New Year reception
questions.credit: Admiral Dewey and officers of the Navy in line at President Roosevelt's New Year reception, 1902. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What did he do the moment the official line ended?
options: Went straight to bed
Called an emergency cabinet meeting
Shook hands with every aide, usher and policeman in sight
Refused to shake another hand for a week
questions.explanation: Still unsatisfied, he worked his way round the aides, ushers and policemen who had spent the day managing the crowd. Only then did he go upstairs and scrub himself clean. Later that afternoon he took his wife and five of the six children out for a ride in the country.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt shaking hands with veterans of the Spanish-American War
questions.credit: The Colonel shaking hands with veterans of the Spanish War. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: News reached him during the 1905 reception that changed the shape of a war. What was it?
options: Port Arthur had surrendered
Britain had declared neutrality
The Panama Canal route had been approved
The Russian fleet had reached the Pacific
questions.explanation: John Hay discreetly murmured that Port Arthur had fallen, and Roosevelt promptly trumpeted it to the assembled diplomats — including the Russian ambassador, who had not yet heard and had to keep smiling his way down the line. Within a year Roosevelt had brokered the peace that ended the Russo-Japanese War and won him the Nobel Prize.
questions.imageAlt: The East Room of the White House, 1903
questions.credit: The East Room, the grand reception room of the White House, 1903. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: As governor, he held a New Year's reception in Albany in 1900. Who pointedly stayed away?
options: Elihu Root, then Secretary of War
Mark Hanna, the Republican national chairman
President William McKinley himself
Thomas Platt, the state Republican boss
questions.explanation: Platt — the "Easy Boss" who had reluctantly made him governor — skipped it to register disapproval of Roosevelt's plans for the new year, which included regulating large corporations and making them disclose their earnings. Platt's solution was to kick him upstairs into the vice presidency. Hanna's response is famous: only one life would then stand between that madman and the presidency.
questions.imageAlt: The New York State Assembly composite portrait
questions.credit: New York State Assembly, 1882-1884. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: How fast could he work a receiving line?
options: He never hurried; about ten a minute
About sixty hands a minute
About two hundred hands a minute
About six hands a minute
questions.explanation: One reporter clocked him at roughly sixty a minute — a hand a second, sustained for hours. He had a technique: take the other person's hand quickly, keep it moving, and never let anyone get a grip on you.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt shaking hands with a line of veterans
questions.credit: The Colonel shaking hands with veterans of the Spanish War. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Who stood beside him through these receptions?
options: Nobody — he received alone
His sister Bamie
His daughter Alice
Edith
questions.explanation: Edith, every time. She was fiercely private about her marriage and shared almost nothing of him with anyone, but she understood that he was a public man and took her place in the line without complaint. Her first turn as White House hostess came at the reception welcoming 1902.
questions.imageAlt: Portrait of Edith Kermit Carow Roosevelt
questions.credit: Edith Kermit Carow Roosevelt. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: He threw open Sagamore Hill to his Oyster Bay neighbours after his first summer as president. How were they invited?
options: They were not — they simply turned up
By engraved card to every household
Through the newspapers and announcements at local churches
By a notice nailed to the post office door
questions.explanation: Word went out in the papers and from the pulpits, and more than eight thousand people came up the hill. They ate gingersnaps on the lawn while Roosevelt, in a frock coat, worked the line for two hours and told everyone he was "dee-lighted" to see them. Asked afterwards how tired he must be, he said not a bit.
questions.imageAlt: Interior of Sagamore Hill with elephant tusks, antlers and a bison head
questions.credit: Interior of Sagamore Hill with elephant tusks, antlers and bison head. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.
